profiles.meeting_scenario: Two weeks before launching their hospital's first three Mako robotic arm-assisted total hip arthroplasties using the direct anterior approach, the arthroplasty lead surgeon and the orthopedic service line manager meet to plan the rollout workflow. The context is a community hospital expanding its adult reconstruction program after board approval, with a vendor clinical specialist available remotely and a radiology protocol supposedly already set up. The agenda is to confirm what preparation is needed before the first cases, who owns each step of imaging and pre-op planning, which staff need training, and what should happen in the final 48 hours before surgery. The expected outcome is a shared implementation plan covering responsibilities, scheduling, and timing for imaging, plan review, team preparation, and a pre-launch dry run.

members.name: Dr. Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Primary and revision total hip arthroplasty, direct anterior approach, component positioning, perioperative arthroplasty pathway design
members.background: Recently recruited from a tertiary referral center where she performed high-volume direct anterior THA and used Mako for selected hip cases during fellowship and early attending practice.
members.private_state: She wants the launch to feel controlled and low-friction so the first few cases go smoothly and do not erode surgeon confidence in the new robotic program; she is especially concerned about preserving surgeon decision-making around implant planning without creating extra meetings or OR delays.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the pre-op plan is uploaded, they mean the surgeon-reviewed and clinically finalized Mako plan is in the system, not just a draft prepared from CT data.
Most of the non-scrub perioperative workflow for direct anterior THA is already familiar enough that only the immediate OR field team needs special robotic training.
The hospital's 'Mako hip CT protocol' refers to the same pelvis-to-condyles protocol she used previously for robotic THA planning.
A dry run for a new robotic hip workflow is primarily a brief sequence and software check with the rep and lead tech, not a full physical OR simulation.

members.name: Jordan Lee
members.expertise: Perioperative implementation, OR scheduling, multidisciplinary training coordination, vendor logistics, radiology-to-OR workflow setup
members.background: Oversees joint program operations across perioperative services and previously helped stand up robotic knee and spine workflows, but has not launched a direct anterior robotic hip pathway with this surgeon before.
members.private_state: Jordan wants the launch to appear organized and compliant across departments, avoid last-minute operational surprises, and demonstrate that the service line can operationalize new technology without repeated escalation.
hidden_assumptions: If the CT study and patient shell are loaded and the vendor can generate the case template, that counts as the pre-op plan being uploaded for planning purposes.
Any new robotic arthroplasty workflow automatically includes all downstream departments touched by the case, even if the surgeon only mentions the OR team.
The 'Mako hip CT protocol' already on file from the implementation kickoff is the standard protocol everyone means unless someone explicitly requests a revision.
A dry run for a first-in-program robotic case means a physical in-room rehearsal with equipment, positioning, tray flow, and support services involved.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the pre-op plan being uploaded
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the 'pre-op plan will be uploaded the day before.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the surgeon-approved final Mako planning file is completed after she personally reviews cup position, stem selection, leg length, and offset no later than 5 PM the day before surgery.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the patient's CT-based case shell and vendor-generated draft template are loaded into the system by the prior afternoon, even if surgeon review happens later or informally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are used to a mixed clinical-administrative workflow and the phrase sounds binary and routine; because each assumes the other shares the same implementation norm, neither thinks to distinguish draft availability from final surgical sign-off.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in team training
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to schedule 'team training' before the first cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a focused session for the immediate operative team: scrub nurse, circulator, first assist, and possibly the vendor specialist for robotic sequence review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader rollout session including OR staff plus anesthesia, radiology, sterile processing, PACU, and physical therapy because all touch the new robotic hip pathway.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each speaker hears familiar role names that overlap with their own mental boundary, so the phrase 'team' feels naturally aligned even though one assumes a narrow room-based team and the other assumes the full perioperative chain.

misalignment_points.topic: Which CT protocol is being referenced
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use 'the low-dose Mako hip CT protocol radiology already has.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the specific robotic THA protocol she knows from prior practice: pelvis through distal femoral condyles with standardized lower-extremity positioning notes used for hip version and leg-length planning in direct anterior THA.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the hospital's existing implementation document labeled as the Mako hip protocol from a prior vendor kickoff, a shorter low-dose order set that radiology filed for robotic joint imaging and treats as the current approved version.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The two documents share nearly identical shorthand labels and both parties assume there is only one official protocol in circulation, so saying 'the protocol radiology already has' creates false certainty instead of prompting comparison.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to do a 'dry run on Monday' before the first live case.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a short desktop workflow check covering plan review, implant library confirmation, and the sequence of robotic steps with the lead scrub and rep.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an after-hours in-room rehearsal with the Hana table, draping setup, tray pull, array placement supplies, and participation from support departments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have prior implementation experience where 'dry run' was standard shorthand, and because they also agree on the timing and intent, the conversation never naturally forces them to define whether it is virtual, tabletop, or physical.

turns.inner_thought: I need these first three cases to feel boring in the best possible way. If the workflow is lean and the plans are truly finalized ahead of time, the first day will go smoothly and nobody will lose confidence in the program. I do not want this to turn into a huge operational production with extra checkpoints that slow down decision-making.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want the first three robotic direct anterior hips to feel tightly controlled, especially that first Wednesday case. If we can map exactly what needs to happen beforehand and who owns each piece, I think we can keep the launch clean.

turns.inner_thought: This has to look organized across every department touched by the case. The last thing I want is a day-before scramble because one downstream group wasn't looped in. If we lock imaging, training, vendor support, and the final checkpoints now, we can show the service line can operationalize this without escalation.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. From the operations side, I’d like us to lock down imaging, training, vendor coverage, and the final pre-case checkpoints this week so there aren’t any surprises as we get closer.

turns.inner_thought: For me this is simple if radiology uses the pelvis-to-condyles low-dose robotic hip CT I know, and if the pre-op plan is uploaded the day before after I’ve personally reviewed cup position, stem choice, leg length, and offset. Once that finalized plan is in, the OR side should be familiar enough.
turns.utterance: From my standpoint, if radiology is using the low-dose Mako hip CT protocol radiology already has, and the pre-op plan is uploaded the day before, the surgical side should be pretty straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that matches what I have on file: the existing low-dose Mako hip protocol approved last month. And if the CT is done, the patient shell is loaded, and the vendor has the template in by the prior afternoon, I can count the pre-op plan as uploaded for planning purposes. That should satisfy readiness.
turns.utterance: That should be workable. Radiology can use the low-dose Mako hip CT protocol radiology already has, and the vendor should have the pre-op plan uploaded by the prior afternoon.

turns.inner_thought: I only need the people actually in the room to know the robotic sequence cold: scrub, circulator, first assist, maybe the rep. I don’t want a giant rollout meeting that adds noise. A concise session should be enough to make the first cases low-friction.
turns.utterance: I’d also like to schedule team training next week. I’m thinking something concise and practical, really centered on the robotic sequence for the people in the room during the case.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. Team training needs to include the whole perioperative chain, not just the OR core. Anesthesia, sterile processing, PACU, PT, and imaging all touch this workflow, and if any one of them is out of sync, it reflects on the rollout.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I’ll set up team training next week and include anesthesia, sterile processing, PACU, PT, and imaging as well so the whole team is aligned for launch.

turns.inner_thought: As long as Monday gives me a quick check with the lead tech and rep that the planning workflow is clean, the implant library is right, and the robotic sequence is clear, that’s enough. I do not need a big in-room exercise unless something looks off.
turns.utterance: And before we go live, I’d like to do a dry run on Monday, mainly to make sure the planning workflow and the intraoperative sequence are clean.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. A dry run should be a real after-hours rehearsal in the room, with equipment, table setup, trays, and support services present. That’s the safest way to flush out issues before first case and show this launch is being handled properly.
turns.utterance: I can make that happen. I’ll reserve an OR after hours on Monday and have the Hana table, trays, and support staff available for the dry run.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll own choosing the right first patients and I need final say on each plan once it’s ready. Jordan can handle CT orders, scheduling, and the vendor interface. As long as radiology uses the protocol I expect and the plan is actually finalized before the day ends, I’m comfortable.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I’ll take patient selection and the final surgeon review of each plan. If you can coordinate CT ordering, scheduling, and vendor logistics, we should be in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: Great, we have an implementation plan: CTs under the existing protocol already filed with radiology, broad team training next week, the pre-op plans loaded by Tuesday, and a full Monday rehearsal completed. That should cover readiness and keep everyone accountable.
turns.utterance: Perfect. So the CTs will go under the low-dose Mako hip CT protocol radiology already has, team training will happen next week, and by Tuesday the pre-op plans and the Monday dry run should both be complete. I’ll send out the timeline and owners this afternoon.
